Opening

BUILD · SCIENCE · W14A · 2 MINUTES

Autumn Science Review Map

Learning objective

I can organise science records by topic and explain what each can and cannot show.

Success looks like

  • Keep skeleton, nutrition and rock evidence attached to the right topic.
  • Link a record to one cautious claim.
  • Keep a specific limit or missing record visible.

Build a map that helps a reader follow the science. Keep each topic, record and limit connected.

W14A · one 40-minute lesson

Seven stages, with one arrival and one exit. Use the route that helps you show your science today.

No earlier worksheet is needed. Fresh evidence is included.

Point, speak, sign, move cards, draw, write or direct an adult. Use one response mode; no separate participation form.

Arrival

BUILD · SCIENCE · W14A · 4 MINUTES

Four clues to start

Choose a route. Four checks help your teacher decide what support is useful today.

Supported · 4 questions

1. Topic

A skull diagram belongs to body science or rocks?

Help beside the question
Use the topic heading.

Answer guidance

Answer: Body science.

2. Compare

P 4 g; Q 9 g per 100 g: which is lower?

Help beside the question
Both have the same basis.

Answer guidance

Answer: P.

3. Test

Visible holes: has a water test been done?

Help beside the question
Read R1: no water test.

Answer guidance

Answer: No.

4. Source

Are these supplied cards your old class work?

Help beside the question
They say fictional practice.

Answer guidance

Answer: No.

Standard · 4 questions

1. Structure

What function is named on S1?

Help beside the question
Read the caption.

Answer guidance

Answer: Protection of the brain.

2. Basis

What comparison basis is retained in N1?

Help beside the question
Quantity per food amount.

Answer guidance

Answer: Grams of sugar per 100 g.

3. Claim

What does R2 support?

Help beside the question
Keep the stated method.

Answer guidance

Answer: D had no indentation after wiping under that method.

4. Missing

What should happen to an absent class record?

Help beside the question
Do not recreate it.

Answer guidance

Answer: Mark missing and identify an appropriate later check.

Stretch · 4 questions

1. Distinguish

How is a record different from evidence for a question?

Help beside the question
Evidence has a stated use.

Answer guidance

Answer: A record becomes evidence when used to address a particular question.

2. Boundary

Why cannot N1 diagnose a person’s diet?

Help beside the question
It gives two product labels only.

Answer guidance

Answer: It contains no whole-diet or health evidence.

3. Transfer

What can connect N1 and a controlled rock test?

Help beside the question
Reasoning move, not shared conclusion.

Answer guidance

Answer: Both require a stated consistent comparison basis.

4. Plan

Does R3 prove a completed permeability test?

Help beside the question
Its final cells are blank.

Answer guidance

Answer: No; it is a plan.

Starter

BUILD · SCIENCE · W14A · 3 MINUTES

One word, three different topics

A rock test and a sugar-label comparison both use “same basis”. Can their science conclusions be merged?

No answer chosen yet. Think or discuss first.

I do

BUILD · SCIENCE · W14A · 5 MINUTES

Make the science visible

Predict, model, explain

This record shows __. It supports __. It cannot establish __.

Choose each view. Describe the evidence before giving a conclusion.

Keep skeleton/body, nutrition and rock records under their topic headings. These examples are fictional practice.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

All supplied cards below are fictional classroom examples for practice, not recovered pupil records. They can support new reasoning shown today but do not prove a previous practical occurred. Existing genuine records may be used with local school approval. Keep source and method visible; never invent pupil quotations, dates, test values or missing evidence. Skeleton conclusions do not transfer to nutrition or rocks merely because words overlap.

Local explainer · 32 seconds · silent with captions

Use instead of part of the demonstration. It never autoplays and needs no internet.

Full text / no-video alternative

00–08 seconds · Three topics, clear sources
Keep skeleton/body, nutrition and rock records under their topic headings. These examples are fictional practice.

08–16 seconds · Read the exact record
The model skull card labels protection of the brain. The label comparison uses grams of sugar per 100 g.

16–24 seconds · Add a cautious claim
The fictional labels show 4 g and 9 g of sugar per 100 g. That compares these labels, not anyone’s health.

24–32 seconds · Add a limit
Use source, question, claim and limit. Mark missing class evidence honestly instead of recreating it.

Use only school-approved existing records or the clearly labelled fictional practice cards. No new scratch, water, food or body practical is needed. Never restage, backdate or invent a missing record or quotation. Do not ask for personal diets, health or family details. A photograph or completed sheet alone is not proof of independent learning.

We do

BUILD · SCIENCE · W14A · 8 MINUTES

Use the evidence together

Use a clue; explain the group

Select a card, then select its group. Keyboard, pointing and paper routes work too. You can move a card when your reasoning changes.

Skeleton / body science

Nutrition / labels

Rocks / test evidence

Select a card, then choose a group.

Would a small change help? · optional

You may ask for a clearer diagram, fewer cards at once, reading help or more thinking time. Tell your teacher, ask privately, point or pass. Your teacher will say what can change and check whether it helped. No extra sheet is needed.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

S1 supports named protection; N1 supports P<Q per 100 g; R2 supports no groove under the stated method. None proves a person’s health or an unperformed test.

You do

BUILD · SCIENCE · W14A · 16 MINUTES

Show your science

Use today’s evidence

Fresh evidence desk

Choose the digital choices or matching paper. You do not need to complete both.

FICTIONAL PRACTICE RECORDS. These are not evidence that your class completed an earlier activity. Use them to practise reviewing; use actual approved records separately where available.

Practice sourceRecord / observationQuestion it can address
S1Skull named; brain protection captionWhich structure has this protective role?
N1P 4 g; Q 9 g sugar per 100 gWhich supplied label has less sugar on the same basis?
R1Visible holes; no flow testWhich visible feature is present?

Read source and topic.
Choose the question the record addresses.
Add a cautious claim and limit.
Link a shared reasoning move, not unrelated conclusions.

Supported · build your explanation

1. Sort

Sort the nine practice cards into three topics.

Help: Read one card at a time.

2. Link

Choose one card per topic and complete the frame.

Help: It shows __; it cannot show __.

3. Gap

Identify one question the chosen cards cannot answer.

Help: A visible feature is not a hidden-property test.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Body S1/S2/S3; nutrition N1/N2/N3; rocks R1/R2/R3. Accept a matching claim and a genuine limit for each topic.

Standard · build your explanation

1. Select

Choose two supplied records per topic.

Help: Keep their IDs visible.

2. Explain

Add one cautious claim and a specific limit per topic.

Help: Keep label basis or test method.

3. Connect

Add one labelled reasoning link between topics.

Help: Do not merge the scientific conclusions.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

S1 supports named protection; N1 supports P<Q per 100 g; R2 supports no groove under the stated method. None proves a person’s health or an unperformed test.

Stretch · build your explanation

1. Evaluate

Compare the usefulness of one record per topic for a named question.

Help: Source, method, basis and missing details.

2. Connect

Defend one cross-topic link and reject one false link.

Help: Common reasoning is not common results.

3. Audit

Keep one missing or uncertain item visible.

Help: No reconstructed quotation or staged practical.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Accept evaluation tied to source and question. A valid link is controlled comparison. An invalid link uses a rock test to infer diet quality. Missing work remains missing.

Match a claim to its evidence

Use the digital choices or the matching paper page. One response mode is enough.

Revisit the model

Keep skeleton/body, nutrition and rock records under their topic headings. These examples are fictional practice.

Refine one explanation

Check that the explanation follows the supplied observation and keeps the stated limit.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

S1 supports named protection; N1 supports P<Q per 100 g; R2 supports no groove under the stated method. None proves a person’s health or an unperformed test.

Knowledge organiser

BUILD Science · W14A · Shared resource

Learning objective

I can organise science records by topic and explain what each can and cannot show.

Key words

record — A saved observation, diagram or result.

evidence — A record used to answer a stated question.

claim — An explanation supported by evidence.

limit — What the evidence cannot establish.

Remember

  • Skeleton records link named structures to support, protection or movement.
  • Nutrition label comparisons use the same basis and units.
  • Rock descriptions and controlled test results answer different questions.
  • Fictional examples are practice; missing class evidence stays missing.

Success looks like

  • Keep skeleton, nutrition and rock evidence attached to the right topic.
  • Link a record to one cautious claim.
  • Keep a specific limit or missing record visible.

This record shows __. It supports __. It cannot establish __.

Current stage

Preparation and access

Use only school-approved existing records or the clearly labelled fictional practice cards. No new scratch, water, food or body practical is needed. Never restage, backdate or invent a missing record or quotation. Do not ask for personal diets, health or family details. A photograph or completed sheet alone is not proof of independent learning.

Scientific care

All supplied cards below are fictional classroom examples for practice, not recovered pupil records. They can support new reasoning shown today but do not prove a previous practical occurred. Existing genuine records may be used with local school approval. Keep source and method visible; never invent pupil quotations, dates, test values or missing evidence. Skeleton conclusions do not transfer to nutrition or rocks merely because words overlap.

Responsive feedback within teaching

The lesson teacher hears an optional request, explains what can change, tries it and checks the effect. Passing or asking privately is valid. No compulsory participation task or new pupil form. Do not infer assessment codes from a click, download or written box.

W14A · Pupil resource · unmarked · Made by Matt

BUILD Science · Sugar Evidence: Read the Label · Supported

Your task

1. Use these fictional teaching cards. All give sugar in g per 100 g: A — 4 g; B — 9 g; C — 14 g; D — 23 g.

Help with this question

Use a paper strip to track one card at a time. Say or point to the letter, the sugar number and ‘g per 100 g’ together.

2. Put the four cards in order from LEAST sugar per 100 g to MOST. Point, move paper cards or direct an adult.

Help with this question

Compare two numbers first. Place the smaller one towards LEAST, then find where each remaining card belongs.

3. Complete: Label ___ has the least sugar per 100 g. Label ___ has the most.

Help with this question

Look at the two ends of your own order. Use those card letters to fill the gaps.

4. Choose the claim we can support: 'A has less sugar per 100 g than D' / 'A is the healthiest food for everyone'.

Help with this question

Ask: does this sentence describe the sugar evidence, or claim to know everything about the food?

5. Finish or point: These sugar numbers show ONE PART OF NUTRITION / THE WHOLE EATING PATTERN. Keep “g per 100 g” with each number.

Help with this question

Look at what was measured. Think about whether these cards show every nutrient and everything a person eats.

BUILD Science · Sugar Evidence: Read the Label · Standard

Your task

1. Read these fictional teaching labels. Each is PER 100 g. A: carbohydrate 22 g; of which sugars 4 g. B: carbohydrate 67 g; of which sugars 9 g. C: carbohydrate 58 g; of which sugars 14 g. D: carbohydrate 72 g; of which sugars 23 g.

Help with this question

Track the ‘of which sugars’ row. Keep the carbohydrate and sugar rows separate.

2. Make a results row for each label. Copy the SUGAR value with its unit and basis; do not copy total carbohydrate.

Help with this question

Use the headings Label | Sugar / g per 100 g. Check each copied value against its nutrient name.

3. Order A–D from least to most sugar per 100 g.

Help with this question

Check adjacent pairs: is each value no larger than the next? Recheck that all four use the same basis.

4. Write or say one comparison: 'Label ___ has ___ g sugar per 100 g. This is less/more than ___.'

Help with this question

Build the comparison from two complete readings. Include which label you are comparing it with.

5. Explain one thing these sugar numbers cannot tell us about the whole food or eating pattern.

Help with this question

Choose one missing piece of information. Explain why that missing information limits a wider judgement.

BUILD Science · Sugar Evidence: Read the Label · Stretch

Your task

1. Fictional labels, all PER 100 g: A — carbohydrate 22 g, sugars 4 g; B — carbohydrate 67 g, sugars 9 g; C — carbohydrate 58 g, sugars 14 g; D — carbohydrate 72 g, sugars 23 g.

Help with this question

Identify the nutrient and reference amount before selecting numerical evidence.

2. Extract the four sugar values and order them. Keep the unit and basis.

Help with this question

Audit the completed order against the source labels; a correct number copied from the wrong row is still the wrong evidence.

3. Extra label E says 'sugars 3 g per 25 g serving'. Someone puts E before A because 3 is less than 4. Audit this decision.

Help with this question

Compare the reference quantities before comparing the two bare numbers.

4. Put E on a per-100 g basis before comparing. How many 25 g servings make 100 g? Then place E among A–D.

Help with this question

Find the scale factor from 25 g of food to 100 g of food. Apply the same factor to the sugar amount.

5. Write one supported comparison from A–D and repair this claim: 'The lowest-sugar card proves the best food for everybody.'

Help with this question

Separate a justified numerical comparison from a wider judgement. State exactly what the evidence establishes and what it leaves unknown.
